newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Banks still out for reach for big S.Korean groups.
newsitem.headline: Banks still out for reach for big S.Korean groups.

text.p: South Korean business groups are not expected to be allowed to enter the banking business despite a presidential panel's proposal to allow individuals to own up to 10 percent of bank shares, analysts said on Monday.
The Presidential Commission for Financial Reform has proposed lifting the individual ownership ceiling of banks to 10 percent from the current four percent.

The panel said the current 15 percent limit for provincial banks would stay unchanged, but that the new 10 percent ceiling would be applied to newly opened banks or other financial institutions shifting into banking.

Bank ownership by big business groups, or "chaebols", is among the most controversial issues considered by the panel, set up by President Kim Young-sam in January to develop a blueprint for reforming the country's outdated financial sector.
Analysts and economists said the reform plan would make it difficult for chaebols to get into banking without the government's approval. And that, they said, was unlikely.
"It's difficult to say chaebols were given a go-ahead to own banks," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
"The government is unlikely to want to let go of its control of the banking industry. This has been the most effective way of governing chaebols."
The South Korean government has a long tradition of controlling chaebols through their access to credit.
Letting go of that control would be risky, analysts said.

"In the near term, it could help boost competitiveness of banks, burdened by a mountain of bad debt, by establishing a more responsible management," said Kim Byong-seok, a banking analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities. "But in the longer term, chaebols may use banks as their personal cashiers and pressure them to give preferential loans to their financially stricken affiliates," he said.
"Moreover, chaebols could force banks to cut credit lines to their rival companies."
Analysts and economists said the reform panel's proposal called for a screening process that would prevent chaebols from accumulating bank shares.
The Finance Ministry would screen applicants until a separate supervisory committee was set up, the proposal said.
The commission proposal said prior government approval would be required for anyone seeking to obtain more than four percent of a bank's stock.

Financial authorities would evaluate applicants' qualifications, including management ability, credibility and financial status, before allowing them to own more than four percent, the commission proposal said.

The proposal explicitly stated that the government would seek to prevent monopolies. Authorities would also monitor how funds to buy additional stocks were raised and whether the applicant planned a merger or management changes after acquiring more stocks, it said.
"The screening process would make it difficult for chaebols to become bank owners," said an adviser to the commission who asked not to be identified.
"The government wants to prevent a larger concentration of power in an economy dominated by chaebols," he said.
The commission is to present its proposals to President Kim Young-sam on Friday. They will be reviewed by the Finance Ministry before being introduced to parliament in June.
With little opposition expected, analysts said the proposals could be enacted in the second half of the year.
